newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says START-2 must be sealed before new talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says START-2 must be sealed before new talks.

text.p: The United States is determined that its START-2 strategic arms treaty with Russia should be ratified before negotiations open on further nuclear cuts, Secretary of State Warren Christopher said on Friday.

Christopher was commenting in an interview on a Washington Post report that the United States was considering a proposal to circumvent the Russian parliament's reluctance to ratify START-2 by "leaping ahead" to a START-3 round.
The Post said on Thursday that the proposal, favoured by European governments, would help to alleviate Russia's concerns about U.S. superiority in submarine-launched missiles.
But Christopher told news agency reporters: "Our position is that START-2 should be ratified and implemented."

"Certainly our long-term goal is for additional arms control agreements, but I don't think you can leapfrog over START-2, and we've let the Russians know that we want to encourage them to find a basis to go forward with START-2."
START-2, which slashes U.S. and Russian long-range nuclear arsenals by some two thirds to about 3,500 warheads apiece, was signed in 1993.

But the Russian Duma (parliament) has so far resisted strong pressure to ratify. Russian deputies have raised objections ranging from the cost of implementing the treaty to concerns over U.S. missile defence plans.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns, asked if there was any plan to advance START-3 negotiations at all, said "Not that I'm aware of ... We don't want to begin negotiations on START-3 until the Russian Duma has ratified START-2. I want to be very clear about that."

Arms control experts said, however, they understood that in order to spur the Duma to ratify START-2, the administration was seriously considering making a commitment that START-3 negotiations would begin immediately thereafter.
The U.S. commitment would cite a specific target figure for the new reductions that would leave each side with 2,000-2,500 warheads, the experts said.
The goal was to get this deal in place for announcing at a planned March summit between U.S. President Bill Clinton and Russian President Boris Yeltsin, they said.
